strengths: QuEST addresses an important deployment problem with a coherent approach: selectively fine-tuning temporal and attention-related layers while learning timestep-dependent activation scales. Using model-generated calibration data and updating under 10% of weights makes the approach practically appealing.

The empirical gains are meaningful. In Table 3, W4A4 FID improves over EfficientDM from 10.60 to 5.64 on LSUN-Bedrooms and from 14.34 to 11.76 on LSUN-Churches. Producing recognizable W4A4 Stable Diffusion outputs also demonstrates useful progress beyond the failing Q-Diffusion baseline.

Evaluation covers four models across unconditional, class-conditional, and text-conditioned generation, with 50,000 samples for the main LDM evaluations. Temporal-embedding comparisons, sensitivity experiments, and component ablations provide evidence supporting the design choices.

The manuscript supplies optimizer settings, learning rates, sampling configurations, dataset and baseline citations, and a code link. Its discussion of possible interactions with watermarking and safety checking identifies a relevant consequence of quantizing generative models.
weaknesses: The claimed theoretical contribution is unsound as written. Section 2.3.1 expands an MSE loss with respect to the final activation; this quadratic loss has an exact second-order Taylor expansion regardless of perturbation magnitude. Large perturbations therefore do not establish the asserted breakdown. Moreover, Appendix B's Eq. (10) contains an epsilon-transpose-Hessian-epsilon term, whereas Eq. (5) substitutes an output residual without justification. The argument does not prove the claimed sufficiency of fine-tuning, although this does not invalidate the empirical improvements.

The strongest quality claims exceed the evaluation. Stable Diffusion is assessed only with CLIP Score against Q-Diffusion; this does not establish image fidelity or diversity, and Figure 11 shows substantial W4A4 artifacts. ImageNet results are also mixed: at W4A4, QuEST trails EfficientDM in sFID (7.93 versus 7.75) and IS (202.45 versus 250.90), despite slightly better FID. The manuscript itself questions FID in this setting, leaving general superiority inadequately established.

The distinctive contribution is not sufficiently isolated. Teacher-based fine-tuning and timestep grouping have precedents acknowledged in the manuscript. Tables 6–7 show that adding components helps, but do not establish whether the proposed layer selection outperforms comparable parameter-budget alternatives or whether progressive training improves over joint training. These comparisons matter for attributing the gains to the proposed strategy.

Efficiency evidence is incomplete relative to the claims. Table 7 reduces calibration time from 23.08 to 15.25 GPU-hours but increases memory from 10,334 to 12,450 MB. It lacks a direct time/memory comparison with EfficientDM, the closest fine-tuning baseline, and reports no measured inference acceleration. The disclosed W4A4 configuration also retains 8-bit attention operands and first/last layers, while quantization targets the UNet; deployment claims should consistently reflect this scope.

Reproducibility and clarity need improvement: quantizer initialization and granularity, training batch size, classifier-free guidance settings, and precise model-specific layer selections are insufficiently specified. There are also correctable reporting inconsistencies: Figure 5 highlights 25 timesteps while the text selects 20, and the QALoRA paragraph interprets a decrease in FID as evidence of worse performance. These editorial issues are secondary to the theoretical and experimental concerns.
